page.title: GIMP - Improved Graphical User Interface testing
page.description: GIMP now has automatic tests that use the user interface in the same way as a person.
page.text_excerpt: GIMP DOWNLOAD NEWS ABOUT DOCS PARTICIPATE TUTORIALS DONATE Improved Graphical User Interface testing Previous Post 2026-11-16 by Harsh Verma GIMP has a lot of intertwined menus, dialogs and tools. When we change a part of the interface, another may stop working and sometimes, the problem can be missed until a user reports it. To find these problems early, a new GUI testing platform was implemented. A typical GUI test starts GIMP, clicks menus and buttons, and then checks the result. These tests run automatically each time we merge contributor changes. Why we need them⁠ GIMP already has unit tests. A unit test checks one small part of the code, for example how GIMP reads an XCF file. But our unit tests were not opening a real window. So it coult not tell us if a dialog opens, or if a menu item did its job. Note that GIMP already had tests of GUI code, usually interacting directly with the core code, and sometimes even simulating input devices’ events (pointer movements, clicks, drags…). But nothing can beat interacting with the real interface. Furthermore such legacy tests directly hijacking core code come with their own problems, such as breaking all too often (and not because they detected a bug), all while not being able to detect whole categories of bugs. UI tests check the program as a whole, in the same way as you use it. What the tests do⁠ Each test starts a real GIMP and does one small task. Then it reads the result from GIMP. If the result is not correct, the test fails and tells us what went wrong. We have 13 tests at this time. They check that: GIMP starts and shows its main window. The Welcome dialog opens on the correct tab. It also stays hidden when you turn off “Show on Start”. File > New makes an image with the size you set. File > Export As writes a correct PNG file. page.text_excerpt: Skip to content Navigation Menu Products Developers Businesses Resources Pricing Search / Sign in Sign up openssl openssl Repository navigation Code Issues 1k (1k) Pull requests 685 (685) Discussions Actions Projects Wiki Security and quality Insights [NSF] [CVE-2026-121481] Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() - #33652 #33652 Open nmouha wants to merge 4 commits into openssl:master from nmouha:cve-2026-121481 +59 -2 Lines changed: 59 additions & 2 deletions Conversation33 (33) Commits4 (4) Checks114 (114) Files changed4 (4) Conversation nmouha commented Contributor This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" (CVE-2026-121481) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock(): NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int. The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock(). I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock(). No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int, but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c, which rejected only len > INT_MAX. I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod. Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client. I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable (env:VAR), otherwise the command line will be too long. Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840. Checklist documentation is added or updated tests are added or updated 👍 4 👀 2 ope

page.text_excerpt: Wilson Tovar (krthr) home • blog • poesía • photography • say hi 👋 Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app 19/11/2026 A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. Why fanzines.app exists The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐ │ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°) ├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤ │ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘ I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app. In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server. Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine. Fixing how pages are paired In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. page.text_excerpt: Home Services Contact Blog EN Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram, a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. This month, my team and I at Monumental Labs announced the first end-to-end autonomous CNC stone carving system of its kind. Sebastian Marino, James Darby, and I presented it at Embodied AI NYC, hosted by NY Robotics and ZeroSpace Labs in Brooklyn. This post is a written version of our talk: how our system turns a 3D model and a block of marble into a finished sculpture, with no human in the loop. Sim-to-real: the planned toolpaths in simulation alongside the robot carving them in stone. From simulation to stone: a finishing toolpath on the Stanford bunny (left) and the marble bunny the robot carved from it (right). Why stone, and why now Civic buildings like Penn Station and Grand Central were once expected to be monumental. Stone carving never disappeared, but rising costs pushed it out of ordinary construction. At Monumental Labs we use machine learning, computational geometry, and optimization to cut that cost: de-extinction, not displacement. Our goal is zero humans in the loop during the robotic manufacturing process: a fully automated, end-to-end pipeline built for “lights-out” manufacturing. We will continue to work with artists and designers to decide on the final desired sculpture. After robotic manufacturing, we intend to continue to use a hand finishing carving team for final surface quality refinements. Monumental Labs HQ in Greenpoint, Brooklyn. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads: I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful... ...until recently (October 2026): This is un-fucking-acceptable. There is almost never a product manager handing you a roadmap, no revenue line to follow, and no market to lose. This means that work does not exist unless an engineer invents it. The continuous struggle is to find ways to increase the value our platform provides to the users of the system. A big part of a staff engineer’s job in a platform team is to figure out what the team should build next - I like to call that “inventing work”. Thankfully, the signals that help us to invent work are already out there, and they arrive from four directions - from the systems, from the users, from your organization, and from the industry. What follows is a guide to reading each of them. Signals the System Emits Crash-led Discovery Crashes and their associated postmortems, when done right, are clear signals that tell you what to fix, or what to replace. It is rare for postmortems to point to a new thing to build, but sometimes that does happen if you pay close attention to how users were impacted by crashes, or how they made their processes work while your team fixed a long-running crash.
